name: Arabic
intro: Modern Standard Arabic is the main model for formal writing, research, news and many public contexts. Spoken Egyptian, Levantine and Gulf Arabic are separate companions, not minor pronunciation switches. Learn connected script, short-vowel notation and root-pattern morphology; ordinary advanced texts often omit short vowels. Dialect writing conventions vary.

foundation.name: Arabic
notes: Read and write right to left

Arabic has 28 core letters. Many change appearance according to position. The chart shows forms using connection strokes. ا د ذ ر ز و do not join to the letter following them on the left; a word can therefore contain a visible gap without a space.

Short vowels are fatḥa َ /a/, kasra ِ /i/ and ḍamma ُ /u/. Sukūn ْ marks no following short vowel; shadda ّ marks consonant doubling. Long vowels use ا و ي in appropriate contexts. Hamza ء is a glottal stop with several written seats. ة is tāʾ marbūṭa, and ى is alif maqṣūra.

ح/ه, ع/ء, س/ص, ت/ط and د/ض require separate listening practice. MSA pronunciation differs from dialect pronunciation. Learn short versus long vowels and consonant doubling: they can distinguish words. Vowel marks are useful initially, but ordinary adult texts are largely unvowelled.

Sun letters: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن. After ال, their first sound is doubled and l is not separately pronounced: الشَّمْس (ash-shams), the sun. Moon letters: ا ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي. The l is heard before them: القَمَر (al-qamar), the moon. This pronunciation distinction does not remove ل from the written article.
building: ك + ت + ا + ب → كتاب = book (kitāb). Alif does not join onward, so the final ب is visually separated while remaining in the same word.
ك ت ب is a writing-related root: كَتَبَ = he wrote; كِتَاب = book; كَاتِب = writer; مَكْتَب = office/desk. The root guides recognition but does not guarantee an exact meaning for every pattern.
كتاب → الكتاب = a book → the book. كتاب الطالب = the student’s book. In this iḍāfa possession construction, the first noun normally has neither ال nor tanwīn.
phrases: هل يمكنك أن تكرر، من فضلك؟

sections.title: Script, sounds and word structure
sections.explanation: Arabic is written right-to-left, while numbers and embedded Latin text need careful directional handling. Letters have contextual shapes; some do not join to the following letter. Short vowels are often omitted outside teaching and special texts. Long vowels, pharyngeal sounds, emphatic consonants and gemination require audio. A root supplies a lexical family and a pattern shapes a word, but not every meaning is predictable from morphology alone.
examples: A broken plural must be learned, not generated by one suffix.
Related lexical family; meaning depends on the complete form.
exercises: What belongs on an Arabic noun card?
Vowelled singular, plural, gender, root where useful, meaning and an example.
Can every plural be formed by adding ون?
No. Sound plurals and many broken-plural patterns have distinct distributions.

sections.title: Nominal sentences, agreement and definiteness
sections.explanation: Present nominal sentences can omit an English-style is: التقرير مهم. The definite article ال attaches to the noun and participates in pronunciation assimilation before sun letters. Adjectives follow nouns and agree in relevant features. Nonhuman plurals commonly take feminine singular agreement in standard patterns. An إضافة possession construction links nouns, with definiteness and case relationships determined by the whole phrase.
examples: Nominal sentence without a present copula.
exercises: Why is translating every English is as a separate verb wrong?
Present nominal Arabic predicates normally do not require that copula.
Explain بيانات جديدة.
New data. Nonhuman plural agreement commonly uses a feminine singular adjective.

sections.title: Verbs, negation and mood
sections.explanation: Learn perfect and imperfect stems with person, gender and number patterns. Standard negation includes لا for many nonpast statements, لم with a jussive imperfect for past denial, لن with a subjunctive imperfect for future denial, and ليس for many nominal predicates. Verb-derived forms add semantic relationships but must be learned lexically. Root knowledge does not automatically determine vowel patterns.
examples: I did not read the report.
لم governs a jussive imperfect in standard Arabic.
We will not use this method.
exercises: Distinguish لم and لن.
لم denies a past occurrence; لن denies a future one, with different mood government.
What should a verb card include?
Perfect/imperfect forms, verbal noun where useful, government, derived family and examples.

sections.title: Relatives, formal compression and case
sections.explanation: Standard Arabic has grammatical case and mood endings that may be absent in ordinary unvowelled writing and are often reduced at pauses. Relative pronouns agree with antecedents, while indefinite noun modifiers can use clause patterns without the same explicit relative marker. Long formal sentences require tracking pronoun reference and agreement. MSA production and dialect speech should be kept as distinct register systems.
examples: Feminine relative التي; object suffix ها resumes the method.
تشير إلى is weaker than proving.
exercises: Identify the resumptive reference in نستخدمها.
ها refers to الطريقة, the object of using.
Should dialect negation automatically replace MSA negation in a formal paper?
No. Register and grammatical systems differ.

sections.title: Research reading and professional courtesy
sections.explanation:
Teaching passage: تشير النتائج إلى علاقة بين عاملين. لكنها لا تثبت أن أحدهما يسبب الآخر. يجب مراعاة ظروف الدراسة عند تقييم الاستنتاج.
Translation: The results indicate a relationship between two factors. But they do not prove that one causes the other. The study conditions must be considered when assessing the conclusion. The passage is formal MSA; spoken companions have their own grammar and idiom.
examples: ليس negates the nominal predicate; full vowel notation would expose case endings.
exercises: What should a summary preserve?
Indication of a relationship, denial of causal proof and a requirement to consider conditions.
Write a 100-word formal request.
Use MSA throughout, correct agreement, clear pronoun references and an appropriate salutation.

rules.title: Independent pronouns
rules.explanation: Independent pronouns identify person and number; Arabic also distinguishes gender and dual forms. A present nominal sentence normally has no expressed be verb. Standard and dialect pronoun systems differ.

examples.native: أنا آسف، ولكن هذا لم يعد متاحاً.
examples.translation: I'm sorry, but it's no longer available.

examples.native: أنا أعرف أين يعمل توم.
examples.translation: I know where Tom works.

examples.native: أنا آكل تفاحةً.
examples.translation: I'm eating an apple.

rules.title: Demonstratives
rules.explanation: Demonstratives agree in relevant gender/number distinctions. هذا كتاب is this is a book, whereas هذا الكتاب refers to this book as a phrase. Definiteness affects the structure.

examples.native: هذا أغبى ما قُلتُه على الإطلاق.
examples.translation: That's the stupidest thing I've ever said.

examples.native: أداء هذه السيارة أفضل من تلك.
examples.translation: This car has a better performance than that one.

examples.native: لا يعيش أحد في هذا المنزل.
examples.translation: Nobody lives in this house.

rules.title: Definite article
rules.explanation: الـ marks definiteness and is written attached. Before sun letters its l sound assimilates to the following consonant, which is doubled in pronunciation. Written spelling still retains ال.

examples.native: لا شيئَ مثالي.
examples.translation: Nothing's perfect.

examples.native: صديق في اليد خير من اثنين على الشجرة!
examples.translation: A friend in hand is worth two in the bush!

examples.native: تسلّقت ليلى السّلّم.
examples.translation: Layla climbed the ladder.

rules.title: Adjective and noun agreement
rules.explanation: Attributive adjectives generally follow the noun and agree in gender, definiteness, case and relevant number patterns. Non-human plurals commonly take feminine singular agreement in MSA.

examples.native: ذكر تقرير جديد أن احتمال أن تواجه الفتيات سوء التغذية والفقرَ والعنف والحرمان من التعليم أكثرُ من الأولاد.
examples.translation: Girls are more likely than boys to be malnourished, suffer poverty, face violence and be refused an education, according to a new report.

examples.native: يريد الناس استخدام التقنية الجديد التي توفرت.
examples.translation: People want to use the new technology which is available.

examples.native: أنت مشتر جيد.
examples.translation: You are a good customer.

rules.title: Possession and iḍāfa
rules.explanation: Possessive suffixes attach to nouns. An iḍāfa noun chain expresses another possession relation; its first noun normally has neither the definite article nor tanwīn. Pronunciation differs by dialect and register.

examples.native: هىَ ليست أختي.
examples.translation: She's not my sister.

examples.native: أنا آسف يا محمد، لقد نسيت اسمك!
examples.translation: I'm sorry Mohammed, I forgot your name!

examples.native: هل أستطيع أن أسألك عن اسمك؟
examples.translation: May I ask your name?

rules.title: Past kāna
rules.explanation: كان and its forms establish a past state and participate in other constructions. In fully inflected MSA, kāna affects the case pattern of a nominal predicate. Gender/person distinctions matter.

examples.native: كان سامي يريد شخصا يعتني به.
examples.translation: Sami wanted someone to watch over him.

examples.native: كان فاضل يتمنّى أن يكون ليده ما كان عند ليلى.
examples.translation: Fadil wanted what Layla had.

examples.native: كان سامي يحبّ مساعدة أبي.
examples.translation: Sami liked helping Dad.

rules.title: Negation lā and laysa
rules.explanation: لا negates various verbal/general constructions; ليس negates many nominal predicates. Their grammar is not identical. Dialects use different combinations and should be practised in their own section.

examples.native: توم ليس وحيداً الآن.
examples.translation: Tom isn't lonely now.

examples.native: لا أريد وظيفة بدوام كامل.
examples.translation: I don't want a full-time job.

examples.native: لا وقت للشرح.
examples.translation: There is no time for explanation.

rules.title: Past negation lam
rules.explanation: لم normally negates a past occurrence using a jussive imperfect verb. It is not followed mechanically by an ordinary past form. Unvowelled text hides some mood distinctions.

examples.native: لم يتزوج سامي قطّ.
examples.translation: Sami never married.

examples.native: لم نكن نتقاتل
examples.translation: We weren't fighting.

examples.native: إذا لم تسرع سيفوتك القطار.
examples.translation: If you don't hurry, you'll miss the train.

rules.title: Future negation lan
rules.explanation: لن normally introduces future-oriented negation with a subjunctive imperfect form in MSA. The written particle is separate from the verb. Contrast its time relation with لم.

examples.native: لن أنس مراسلة أمّي.
examples.translation: I will not forget to write to my mother.

examples.native: لن تؤذي ذبابة.
examples.translation: It wouldn't harm a fly.

examples.native: لن يأتي أليس كذلك؟
examples.translation: He won't come, will he?

rules.title: Ma and other negatives
rules.explanation: ما has several functions, including negation, interrogation and relative/content uses. A form match alone cannot decide the function. Inspect the surrounding predicate and the translation.

examples.native: ما زال ذراعي يؤلمني.
examples.translation: My arm still hurts.

examples.native: ما اسم صديقك؟
examples.translation: What's your friend's name?

examples.native: أخذ سامي ما قلته له على محمل الجدّ.
examples.translation: Sami took what I told him to heart.

rules.title: Common verbal predicates
rules.explanation: Arabic verbs encode person, gender, number and aspect/tense series. Imperfect prefixes are part of the agreement pattern. Record a verb’s past, imperfect and verbal noun with a sentence.

examples.native: يريد سامي أن يتقدّم في حياته.
examples.translation: Sami wants to move on with his life.

examples.native: سامي يحبّ رسوم الأنمي الإباحيّة.
examples.translation: Sami likes anime porn.

examples.native: يريد سامي أن يمضي بعض الوقت لوحده.
examples.translation: Sami wants to spend some time alone.

rules.title: Future markers
rules.explanation: MSA uses سوف or prefixed سـ in common future constructions. A prefixed marker is not a separate word in spelling. Dialect future markers differ and belong in the dialect material.

examples.native: سوف يكون عندنا الكثير من الطعام.
examples.translation: We'll have plenty of food.

examples.native: سوف أشتري هديّة لتوم.
examples.translation: I'll buy a gift for Tom.

examples.native: لقد وعدني أنه سيأتي على الساعة الرابعة.
examples.translation: He promised me that he would come at four.

rules.title: Prepositions
rules.explanation: Prepositions mark relations and govern genitive in fully inflected MSA. Their complements can be nouns or pronominal suffixes. English in/on/to choices do not map one-to-one.

examples.native: نشأ سامي في مجتمع مسلم.
examples.translation: Sami grew up in a Muslim community.

examples.native: بإمكانك استخدامها في أي وقت.
examples.translation: You can use it anytime.

examples.native: دُعيتُ إلى حفلة ساتشِكو.
examples.translation: I was invited to Sachiko's party.

rules.title: Relative forms
rules.explanation: Definite relative constructions use forms agreeing with the antecedent. Indefinite noun modification can use a relative-like clause without this same overt relative word. Agreement and referential status both matter.

examples.native: قام توم بنفس الشيء الذي قامت به ماريا
examples.translation: Tom did the same thing Mary did.

examples.native: أراني توم القصائد التي كتبها حين كان مراهقا.
examples.translation: Tom showed me the poems that he'd written when he was a teenager.

examples.native: العباقرة من الناس كالشهبُ التي قُدِّر لها أن تحترق لتضيء زمنها.
examples.translation: Men of genius are meteors destined to burn in order to illuminate their century.

rules.title: Content and purpose
rules.explanation: أن before a verb and أنّ before a nominal clause belong to distinct complement patterns. Purpose can use كي or related structures. Unvowelled أن requires contextual interpretation.

examples.native: هل سبق و أن قمتِ بعرض للتّعرّي؟
examples.translation: Have you ever stripped before?

examples.native: إنه خطر أن تقود بتهور.
examples.translation: It is dangerous to drive so fast.

examples.native: لكل فرد الحق أن يلجأ إلى بلاد أخرى أو يحاول الاتجاء إليها هربا من الاضطهاد.
examples.translation: Everyone has the right to seek and to enjoy in other countries asylum from persecution.

rules.title: Questions
rules.explanation: هل forms many yes/no questions; other words request specific information. من can be who or from, depending on structure and pronunciation. Preserve the intended question relation.

examples.native: "هل قبلتها؟" "نعم، قبلتها.
examples.translation: "Did you kiss her?" "Yes, I kissed her."

examples.native: متى يمكننا الأكل؟
examples.translation: When can we eat?

examples.native: هل خرجت ليلة الأمس؟
examples.translation: Did you go out last night?

rules.title: Conditions
rules.explanation: إذا commonly frames expected/real conditions, إن conditional patterns with specific MSA mood rules, and لو many counterfactuals. These are not freely interchangeable English if equivalents.

examples.native: غيري العلم، لو سمحت.
examples.translation: Change the flag, please.

examples.native: ”أنا أكرهكِ.“ ”طلّقني إذا. “
examples.translation: "I hate you." "Divorce me then."

examples.native: الأعداد الأولية مثل الحياة، منطقية تمامًا، لكن يستحيل إيجاد القواعد لها، حتى لو أمضيت وقتك كله تفكر فيها.
examples.translation: Prime numbers are like life; they are completely logical, but impossible to find the rules for, even if you spend all your time thinking about it.

rules.title: Cause and concession
rules.explanation: لأن supplies a reason; لكن introduces contrast; لذلك a consequence. Attached pronouns and nominal clauses affect the surrounding grammar. Distinguish argument relationships carefully.

examples.native: لكن لديك أطفال.
examples.translation: But you have kids.

examples.native: كان سامي بحاجة لذلك المال.
examples.translation: Sami needed the money.

examples.native: أنا تلميذ، ولكن هو ليس بواحد.
examples.translation: I am a student, but he isn't.

rules.title: Coordination and quantification
rules.explanation: و is usually attached to the following written word; أو marks alternatives. كل/بعض create quantity phrases with their own agreement and possession-like relations. A separate single و is not the normal spelling in connected prose.

examples.native: لقد وصلتَ للتّو.
examples.translation: You have only just arrived.

examples.native: كلا سامي و ليلى مسلمين.
examples.translation: Sami and Layla are both Muslim.

examples.native: انتهى كل شيء.
examples.translation: Everything's done.

rules.title: Courtesy and certainty
rules.explanation: ربما limits certainty, يمكن expresses possibility/ability in suitable constructions, and يجب expresses obligation/necessity. Professional Arabic distinguishes a supported claim from a proposed explanation.

examples.native: يجب ان تذهب للبيت ؟
examples.translation: Shouldn't you go home?

examples.native: اتصل بي حين تأتي إلى طوكيو رجاءً.
examples.translation: Please get in touch with me when you come to Tokyo.

examples.native: مازال يجب دفع الفاتورة اليوم.
examples.translation: The bill still has to be paid today.

dialects.name: Arabic - Egyptian
dialects.target: Professional spoken use - Egyptian Arabic companion
dialects.intro: This companion uses broadly Cairene Egyptian as a starting model. It does not represent every Egyptian variety. Arabic-script examples have common teaching spellings rather than a single official dialect orthography. Romanised reading aids are optional personal notes. Use MSA for formal research writing and Egyptian for its appropriate spoken contexts.

units.title: Pronunciation and local vocabulary
units.explanation: Cairene ج commonly corresponds to /g/, and ق can be a glottal stop in many everyday words, with lexical and social exceptions. Emphatic and pharyngeal consonants still need careful practice. Egyptian vocabulary and pronunciation are not generated by replacing two letters in an MSA sentence.
examples: A common Egyptian greeting; add appropriate endings for the addressee.
exercises: Is every Egyptian ق automatically a glottal stop?
No. Register, word and speaker can affect realisation.
What should a dialect phrase card record?
Location, addressee, pronunciation model and context.

units.title: Aspect and negation
units.explanation: A b-prefix often marks ordinary indicative/habitual present forms; ongoing activity and future reference have dialect-specific patterns. Egyptian verbal negation commonly surrounds the verb with ما ... ش. مش often negates nominal predicates and appears in other constructions. Do not paste this circumfix onto every MSA verb and assume the result is idiomatic Egyptian.
examples: Male speaker, nominal negation with مش.
exercises: Contrast مش and ما ... ش in the examples.
مش negates a nominal predicate here; the circumfix negates the past verbal form.
What changes for a female speaker saying ready?
جاهزة is the usual feminine adjective form.

units.title: Requests and spoken professional interaction
units.explanation: Learn real exchanges: asking for repetition, checking an appointment, clarifying a price and explaining a delay. Formal workplaces may mix MSA-derived vocabulary with dialect grammar. Choose a natural register from a local model rather than reading a formal MSA email aloud and labelling it Egyptian.
examples: Spoken request with post-nominal demonstrative دي.
Male speaker; محتاجة for a female speaker.
exercises: Role-play a clarification exchange.
Use the request, repeat your understanding and ask whether it is correct. Record it with a model speaker.
Should this dialect replace MSA in all reading?
No. Formal written resources mostly require MSA; dialect texts and speech have their own place.

dialects.name: Arabic - Levantine
dialects.target: Professional spoken use - Levantine Arabic companion
dialects.intro: Levantine covers several communities across Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine. Examples here are broadly compatible teaching forms, with an initial urban central-Levantine orientation. Select a specific community for pronunciation and advanced production. Regional disagreement is not automatically an error.

units.title: Variation, sounds and everyday expressions
units.explanation: Realisation of ق varies across urban, rural and other communities. The same regional label contains different vowels and vocabulary. كيفك and هلّق are common in many central-Levantine models; other communities use alternatives. Learn complete audio-backed exchanges rather than treating Levantine as one uniform accent.
examples: Common in many Syrian/Lebanese contexts; not universal throughout the region.
exercises: What should you choose before advanced accent imitation?
A specific community and model speaker.
Why is a vocabulary difference within Levantine not necessarily wrong?
The regional family includes several established local systems.

units.title: Aspect, future and negation
units.explanation: Many Levantine varieties use b- for indicative/habitual present and عم for ongoing action in appropriate patterns. رح commonly introduces future reference. Negation varies: ما for many verbs, and مو or مش for nominal predicates according to community. Southern varieties can use -ش patterns. Keep one chosen system consistent before expanding comprehension.
examples: Future marker رح with a verb form appropriate to the speaker.
exercises: Should مو and مش be treated as interchangeable in every community?
No. Their distribution depends on locality and construction.
How should an ongoing-action pattern be learned?
From complete local examples with audio and the appropriate use of عم and verb form.

units.title: Requests and interaction
units.explanation: Professional dialect interaction still requires precise clarification and tact. Spoken grammar can carry technical vocabulary from MSA. Use a local request form, check the interlocutor's meaning and state your proposed next step. Formal documents generally remain in MSA.
examples: A common spoken request; local pronunciation differs.
بدي is common in several central-Levantine models.
exercises: Write and record a short clarification dialogue.
Ask, paraphrase, confirm and thank. Keep your chosen community's negation and future patterns consistent.
Does learning this companion cover every Levantine variety?
No. Extend listening systematically to the actual community you need.

dialects.name: Arabic - Gulf
dialects.target: Professional spoken use - Gulf Arabic companion
dialects.intro: Gulf Arabic includes several communities and overlaps with other Arabian varieties. Saudi Arabic is not one homogeneous dialect, and Gulf, Hijazi and Najdi are not interchangeable labels. These notes introduce common Gulf teaching patterns; choose a particular country/community for advanced production. The historical Saudi course in Resources is a separate labelled resource.

units.title: Variation, sounds and everyday words
units.explanation: Realisation of ق can be /g/ in many Gulf speech contexts, with other realisations and formal pronunciations also present. Some communities have affricated realisations of certain consonants in specific contexts. Do not imitate these features from spelling alone. Vocabulary such as الحين for now is common, but not unique or universal across all Arabian speech.
examples: Common in some Gulf communities; alternatives occur.
exercises: Is one Gulf greeting universal in every country?
No. Choose a local model and learn alternative forms for comprehension.
What belongs in a pronunciation note?
Community, word, recorded model and the exact feature being practised.

units.title: Verb systems and negation
units.explanation: Many Gulf systems do not use the Levantine b-prefix as a universal present-tense marker. ما commonly negates verbal predicates, while مب or مو can occur in nominal negation depending on locality. Future markers and ongoing-action constructions differ across communities. MSA-derived words can coexist with dialect morphology.
examples: Common past verbal negative; pronunciation varies.
A nominal negative found in some Gulf systems, not every community.
exercises: Why should you not import Egyptian ما ... ش into every Gulf sentence?
The negative systems differ. Learn the chosen local construction.
How should future reference be studied?
Use an attested local pattern and record its distribution rather than inventing a uniform Gulf rule.

units.title: Professional interaction and register
units.explanation: A clear spoken request can be less formal than its MSA counterpart while remaining courteous. Relationships, workplace culture and community norms determine address and directness. Learn to clarify documents in dialect, but retain MSA competence for the documents themselves.
examples: A widely recognisable spoken pattern with local variation.
A usable request with broadly formal-compatible vocabulary.
exercises: Role-play clarification of an appointment.
Ask for the time, repeat it and confirm location. Match your model community's pronunciation.
What is the distinction between the companion and the historical Saudi course?
The companion maps selected Gulf variation; the source course represents its own explicitly labelled historical variety.

passages.translation: I am learning a new language. Each day, I read a short text and listen to clear examples. I write useful words in a notebook. When I make a mistake, I check the rule and try again. My goal is to understand people and express my ideas clearly.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
